summary.text: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose direction a linear transformation leaves unchanged or reverses, so the transformation only scales it.
The scaling factor is the eigenvalue: the amount an eigenvector is stretched or shrunk, with a negative value meaning the direction is reversed.
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues characterize a transformation, and in a feedback system the largest eigenvalue governs the long-term behavior.

items.prompt: A transformation tilts and lengthens most arrows but leaves every arrow lying along the horizontal axis exactly where it was. What eigenvalue do those horizontal arrows have?

options.label: Zero, since those arrows do not move at all
One, since neither direction nor length changes
Negative one, since they point sideways

items.explain: Points on the horizontal axis keep their direction and their length, so the scaling factor is one.

items.prompt: A transformation sends an arrow to a new arrow that is longer and points in exactly the opposite direction. Is the original arrow an eigenvector?

options.label: No, because its direction changed
No, because it also became longer
Yes, with a negative eigenvalue
Yes, but only with eigenvalue zero

items.explain: An eigenvector may have its direction reversed; that happens when the eigenvalue is negative.

items.prompt: A transformation rotates some arrows, shears others, and merely stretches or shrinks a third group. Which group holds the eigenvectors?

options.label: The arrows that are only stretched or shrunk
The arrows that are rotated
The arrows that are sheared
The arrows that end up longest

items.explain: Eigenvectors undergo neither rotation nor shear; they are only stretched or shrunk.

items.prompt: A system feeds its output back into the same transformation again and again. What tells you where it settles after many rounds?

options.label: The smallest eigenvalue and its vector
The average of all the eigenvalues
The first arrow you started with
The largest eigenvalue and its eigenvector

items.explain: The largest eigenvalue governs long-term behavior, and its eigenvector is the steady state of the system.

items.prompt: Many different vectors are all scaled by the very same factor. Gather them together with the zero vector. What is that collection called?

options.label: An eigenbasis
An eigenspace
A shear mapping
An eigensystem

items.explain: Eigenvectors sharing one eigenvalue, together with the zero vector, form an eigenspace.

items.prompt: A student says eigenvalues only make sense for geometric transformations and cannot be found from a square grid of numbers. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Nothing; matrices cannot have eigenvalues
Only symmetric matrices have eigenvalues
In finite dimensions, either language defines them equally
Matrices only give eigenvalues for two dimensions

items.explain: In a finite-dimensional space, transformations and square matrices correspond directly, so eigenvalues can be defined in either language.

paragraphs.heading: Vectors that keep their direction
paragraphs.text: An eigenvector of a linear transformation is a nonzero vector whose direction the transformation leaves unchanged, or simply reverses. The transformation only scales it by a constant factor λ, so that T𝐯 = λ𝐯. That factor is the eigenvalue, and it can be a negative or even a complex number. The prefix eigen- comes from the German eigen, meaning 'own', 'proper' or 'characteristic', and another name for an eigenvector is a characteristic vector.

paragraphs.heading: The picture with arrows
paragraphs.text: Vectors can be pictured as arrows, each with a length and a direction. A linear transformation can rotate, stretch or shear the arrows it acts on. Its eigenvectors are the arrows that are only stretched or shrunk, with no rotation and no shear. The eigenvalue is the factor of that stretch or shrink, and a negative eigenvalue turns the arrow around.

paragraphs.heading: A sheared Mona Lisa
paragraphs.text: A shear applied to the Mona Lisa shows the idea. Treat each point of the painting as an arrow from the center to that point. The shear moves points in the top half to the right and points in the bottom half to the left, by an amount that grows with their distance from the horizontal line through the middle. Points on that line do not move, so any arrow pointing straight right or left keeps both its direction and its length. Those horizontal arrows are eigenvectors, each with eigenvalue one.

paragraphs.heading: In the language of matrices
paragraphs.text: For an n × n matrix A and a nonzero vector 𝐯, if A𝐯 is just 𝐯 scaled by a number λ, then 𝐯 is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ, written A𝐯 = λ𝐯. Once a basis is chosen for an n-dimensional vector space, linear transformations of that space correspond directly to n × n square matrices. So in finite dimensions it makes no difference whether eigenvectors are defined with transformations or with matrices. For a matrix, the eigenvectors are n × 1 matrices.

paragraphs.heading: Functions and eigenspaces
paragraphs.text: Eigenvectors need not be arrows at all. If the transformation is the differential operator d/dx, its eigenvectors are functions, called eigenfunctions, as in d/dxe^λx = λe^λx. All the eigenvectors that share one eigenvalue, together with the zero vector, make up an eigenspace. If a set of eigenvectors forms a basis of the transformation's domain, that basis is called an eigenbasis.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors characterize a transformation, so they matter wherever linear algebra is used, from geology to quantum mechanics. Often a system is described by a transformation whose outputs are fed back in as its inputs. In that kind of feedback, the largest eigenvalue governs the long-term behavior after many repetitions, and its eigenvector is the steady state. Other uses include analyzing stability and vibration, atomic orbitals, facial recognition and diagonalizing matrices.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: Eigenvalues are often introduced through matrices, but historically they arose from quadratic forms and differential equations. In the 18th century Leonhard Euler studied the rotation of rigid bodies and saw the importance of their principal axes, and Joseph-Louis Lagrange realized those axes are the eigenvectors of the inertia matrix. In the early 19th century Augustin-Louis Cauchy used their work to classify quadric surfaces and coined the term characteristic root for what is now called an eigenvalue.
